title: Tea retained for home consumption
unit_long: million pounds of tea retained for home consumption a year
label: Tea retained for home consumption (Statistical Abstract)
note: The whole quantity of tea retained for home consumption: in the Abstract's words, found "by deducting the Quantities Over-Entered, and those Exported subsequently to the payment of the Duties, from the Quantities Entered for Home Consumption in the first instance", from the Board of Trade's Statistical Abstracts, 1846-1938, read from the page images of eleven editions (Nos. 8, 13, 26, 41, 42, 46, 48, 59, 69 and 83); where editions overlap they agree, apart from 1865 (No. 13: 97,834,874 lb; No. 26: 97,834,600), and the latest edition read is used. Ireland is included to March 1923; from 1 April 1923 the figures exclude the Irish Free State. While the tea duty was repealed (22 April 1929 to 20 April 1932) the figures for 1929-32 are imports less re-exports. The quantity doubled between 1846 and 1865 (46.7 to 97.8 million lb), passed 200 million in 1891 and 300 million in 1913, rose from 277 million in 1917 to 388 million in 1919, and was 432 million in 1938.

title: Tea drunk per person
unit_long: pounds of tea retained for home consumption per person a year
label: Tea per head (Statistical Abstract)
note: Tea retained for home consumption (imports less re-exports) divided by the whole population, as printed by the Board of Trade; the first per-head table (No. 14, covering 1852-1866) starts in 1852. Ireland is included to 1922; from 1923 the figures are for Great Britain and Northern Ireland. None given for 1915-18. While the tea duty was repealed (1929-32) the figures are retained imports and not strictly comparable. Editions revised earlier years slightly (by up to 0.03 lb) after each census; the latest edition read is used. The 1938 figure (10.18 lb) is shown as printed but does not agree with the same edition's total retained (431.8 million lb), which gives about 9.1 lb with the population implied by the 1933-37 figures; no later edition reprints the table. From 1941 the Ministry of Food's (later MAFF's) estimated supplies per head are shown as a second line: a different measure (supplies moving into consumption; per head of the civilian population to 1947), which gives 9.3 lb for 1934-38 against 9.5 here. The Abstracts read give no figures for 1939-40. From 1974 a third line gives the tea bought for the home per person from Defra's Family Food surveys (the National Food Survey to 2000): a third measure, leaving out tea drunk outside the home, but it starts at 7.8 lb in 1974, the same as the supplies estimate, and falls to 4.2 lb in 2000 and 2.4 lb in 2024-25. Tea was rationed from July 1940 (two ounces a week, about 6.5 lb a year) to the autumn of 1952.

Tea bought and drunk outside the home is not included, and Defra warns that diary surveys under-report purchases. Financial years from 2001-02 are shown at the year they begin; 2006-2015 are calendar years (the financial year 2015-16 is left out, as it overlaps 2015). 67.6 g a week in 1974 (7.8 lb a year, the same as MAFF's supplies for 1974), 36.2 g in 2000 (4.2 lb), 20.7 g in 2024-25 (2.4 lb).

title: Price of imported tea
unit_long: pence per pound: average value of the tea imported, before duty
label: Average price of tea imported (Statistical Abstract)
note: The average price of all tea imported into the United Kingdom, in pence (old pence, 240 to the pound sterling) per lb, as the Board of Trade's Statistical Abstract printed it in its table of the average prices of articles imported: the value of the year's imports divided by their quantity, before duty. 1865-1870 are "from computed values" and 1871 onwards "from declared values" (the importers' own declarations), so the two parts are not strictly comparable. Read from the page images of Nos. 27, 30, 45, 46, 59 and 66; where editions overlap (1868-72, 1884-90, 1897-98, 1905-11) they agree to the hundredth of a penny. Before 1865 the Abstract gives tea prices only by country of origin (China, India, Japan; drawn as "Price of imported tea by origin, 1854-1864"), and from 1908 (No. 68) by origin only: tea from India and Ceylon and tea from China, drawn as two more lines for 1908-1922 rather than joined to this one. The price fell from 19.9d. a lb in 1865 to 12.6d. in 1882, 9.4d. in 1897 and 7.2d. in 1902, then rose with the war to 16.1d. in 1919. For prices after 1919 see "Wholesale price of tea", a different measure.

title: Price of imported tea by origin, 1854-1864
unit_long: pence per pound: average price, as fixed for the computed real value, of the tea imported from each country, before duty
label: Tea from China (Statistical Abstract No. 13)
note: The average price per lb of tea imported into the United Kingdom from China, from India (Assam) and from Japan, before duty, in old pence, from the Board of Trade's Statistical Abstract No. 13 (1851-1865), table "Average prices, as fixed for the computed real value, of some of the principal articles imported" (exclusive of duty), pp. 36-37, read from the page images (Nos. 11 and 12 print the same figures for the years they share). These are the prices the Customs fixed to compute the real value of imports (the "computed real value", which replaced the old official values in 1854), not the importers' declarations, so they are not joined to the declared values from India and Ceylon and from China of 1908-1922. The table begins in 1854; for 1854 and 1855 it prints one price for tea from China and India together (1s. 3½d. and 1s. 3¹⁄₁₆d., 15.5d. and 15.06d.), and Japan has none until 1859, the year its ports opened to British trade. Tea from China cost 14.5d. a lb in 1856, 20.19d. in 1862 and 18d. in 1864; tea from India (Assam), a smaller trade, cost more: 28.75d. in 1856, 21d. in 1860-62 and 27d. in 1864; tea from Japan fell from 18d. in 1859 to 15.75d. in 1864. The average price of all tea imported, from the same computed values, was 19.88d. in 1865 ("Price of imported tea"). India's 1857 figure is read as 2s. 1⅜d.: the numerator of its fraction is blurred in all three editions.

A wholesale auction price of one kind of tea, not the average value of all tea imported, so it is not joined to "Price of imported tea": in 1913 the auction average was 14.06d. a lb against 9.17d. for the declared value of tea from India and Ceylon. 23.54d. in 1920, 25.23d. in 1923, down to 10.24d. in 1932 (the duty was off tea from 1929 to 1932), back to 19.44d. in 1938.

title: Duty on tea
unit_long: pence of customs duty per pound of tea (the full rate; from 1932 the rate on tea from outside the Empire)
label: Tea duty, full rate (Hansard, Statistical Abstract, Finance Act)
note: The customs duty on a pound of tea, in old pence (12d. = 1s.), each change drawn as a step in the year it was made. 1847-1865 from the Budget debates in Hansard (the old and new rate as the Chancellor gave them): 2s. 2¼d. (26¼d., the duty of 2s. 1d. with 5 per cent added) in 1847 and still in December 1852; 1s. 10d. in the Budget of 18 April 1853 (Gladstone's Budget: the first step of a planned fall to 1s.); 1s. 6d. from 5 April 1854; raised for the Crimean War to 1s. 9d. in April 1855; 1s. 5d. from 6 April 1857; 1s. from April 1863; 6d. in the Budget of 27 April 1865 (Lewis's speech of 1855 gives the 1853 duty as 2s. 2½d.; Gladstone's and Disraeli's give 2s. 2¼d.). 1874-1938 from the Statistical Abstract's customs tariffs (the rate in force on 31 May 1874 and 1 July 1921) and its tables of taxes reduced or increased: 6d. on 31 May 1874 (the tariffs of May 1875 and August 1889 also give 6d., and no change to the tea duty is listed between them). Cut to 4d. on 1 May 1890; 6d. from 6 March 1900; 8d. from 20 April 1904; 6d. from 1 July 1905; 5d. from 14 May 1906; 8d. from 18 November 1914; 1s. (12d.) from 22 September 1915. From 2 June 1919 tea from the British Empire paid less ("Imperial Preference"; five-sixths of the full rate in the 1921 tariff), shown as a second line. "Reduced by one-third" on 15 May 1922 (to 8d.) and "by one-half" on 5 May 1924 (to 4d.); repealed from 22 April 1929; from 20 April 1932 4d. on foreign and 2d. on Empire tea; from 22 April 1936 6d. and 4d.; from 27 April 1938 8d. and 6d. These rates held through the war: in the Finance Bill debate of 22 June 1949 "The duty on tea was 8d. per lb. on foreign tea, and 6d. on Empire tea". The Finance Act 1949 charged 2d. on tea not from the Empire and none on Empire tea from 7 April 1949 (the duty had been paid back as a food subsidy: "no point in raising money on the one hand and paying it away on the other"). The 2d. kept only the Empire's preference; in 1963 it became a protective duty (Import Duties (General) (No. 4) Order 1963), and the Import Duties (General) (No. 11) Order 1963 removed the import duties on tea from 1 January 1964, by an arrangement with the European Economic Community. 1866-1873 come from no source read: no change is drawn between 1865 and the 1874 tariff, both 6d.

title: Overseas trade at the prices of the time, 1854-1938
label: Imports
note: The value of goods imported into and exported from the United Kingdom each year at the prices of the time, in million pounds, from the Board of Trade's Statistical Abstracts, read from the page images of eight editions (Nos. 16, 18, 30, 33, 46, 59, 70 and 83; edition, page and table per year in the data file). Imports are valued as they arrived (cost, insurance and freight), exports as loaded on board ("free on board"); bullion and coin and goods transhipped under bond are left out. Re-exports are goods imported and sent on again ("foreign and colonial produce"), so imports less re-exports is what the country kept. Each row was checked by its own sums (United Kingdom produce + re-exports = all exports; imports less re-exports = net imports, or imports + exports = the total trade). Where editions overlap the latest edition read is used; they agree except 1870, 1885 and 1898, revised later, and 1868, where No. 18 misprints the imports (294,460,214 for 294,693,608). The values of new ships exported were not recorded in 1897-98; manufactured tobacco moved from re-exports to United Kingdom produce in 1892; from August 1914 to June 1917 goods owned by the British or Allied governments were left out; and from 1 April 1923 trade with the Irish Free State is overseas trade and the Free State's own trade is left out. Imports rose from 152 million in 1854 to 769 million in 1913 and 1,933 million in 1920, and were 920 million in 1938; exports of United Kingdom produce were 97, 525 and 471 million. Imports were above exports in every year. These are values, not volumes: for the quantities traded see "Overseas trade, 1800-1938 (at 1913 prices)".

title: Prices since 1800 (Retail Prices Index, long run), 1800-2025
label: Retail Prices Index
note: The ONS's long-run Retail Prices Index (series CDKO), the 'composite price index' it joins from older indexes of the cost of living to the RPI (from 1947), yearly, January 1974 = 100, on a logarithmic axis: equal steps are equal ratios. Prices in 2025 were 118 times those of 1800. Prices fell after the Napoleonic wars (16.3 in 1813, 8.4 in 1850) and moved little for a century (9.2 in 1900); they doubled in the First World War (9.8 in 1914, 19.9 in 1918) and rose to 25.3 in 1920, fell back in the 1920s and early 1930s (15.8 in 1933), and have risen in every year since 1935 but 2009: 3.6 times between 1970 and 1980, 6.0 times between 1980 and 2025.

title: Wages in towns, 1790-1860
label: real wages, 1800-1860
note: Wages before the Board of Trade's index (drawn from 1879 in "Real wage rates, 1879-1938"), 1840 = 100. Money wages: G. H. Wood's index of average wages in towns (1899), the unweighted average of 24 towns and districts (London, Manchester, Glasgow, Dublin, Leeds, Sheffield, the Durham and Northumberland and the South of Scotland coalfields, Monimail in Fife and Glamorgan for rural artisans and labourers...), all trades for which he found figures, agriculture left out; a town's line is led by its staple trade. To 1810 "each year stated may, therefore, best be considered as the middle year of a short period". Real wages: the same over the ONS's long-run Retail Prices Index (to 1810 the mean of the year and those beside it), from 1800 when the RPI begins. Bowley warned in 1900 that "it is unfortunate that we cannot with safety use index numbers of wholesale prices as a measure of the purchasing power of the workman's wages"; the RPI before 1914 is itself joined from older estimates, and 1840 was a dear year (prices fell 24% to 1850), so the real line rises sharply after it. Money wages rose 69% from 1790 to 1810 and fell 19% from 1810 to 1845 (Wood: "the increase (69 per cent.) which took place between 1790 and 1810; the decrease (19 per cent.) between 1810 and 1845"); real wages were 72 in 1800, 96 in 1810 and 138 in 1860. Dots: Bowley's index numbers by decade (1900), "which our work indicates, but which are not yet established", printed on 1890-99 = 100 and drawn here on 1840-50 = 100 at mid-decade, ranges as bars: 67 in the 1780s, 112 in the 1810s, 167 in the 1890s. Wood's printed average for 1860 (116, as Bowley's) is 1.4 below the mean of the towns he prints for that year.

title: Real wage rates, 1879-1938
unit_long: index of wage rates over prices
note: Wage rates divided by prices: what a week's wage at the standard rates would buy, three lines on their own bases. 1879-1913: the Board of Trade's index of the general course of wages (unweighted mean of building, coal mining, engineering, textiles and agriculture), 1900 = 100, over the ONS's long-run Retail Prices Index. 1914-1934: July 1914 = 100, wage rates over the official cost-of-living index at the same date, the band showing the range printed: to 1919 Bowley's rough average of time rates in July (1921), from 1920 the Ministry of Labour's estimate of the average increase in weekly full-time rates at the end of each year (the cost of living at the beginning of the next January). 1924-1938: the Ministry of Labour's index of weekly full-time rates in a representative selection of industries, 1924 = 100, over the RPI. Rates, not earnings: none counts short time, unemployment, overtime or the move of workers into better-paid trades (war work raised earnings well above rates). Real wage rates rose 19% from 1879 to 1900 as prices fell (84.3 to 100), then fell to 96.1 in 1912 as prices rose. In the war prices outran wages (real rates 76 in July 1917, July 1914 = 100); wages caught up in 1918-19 and stood at 104 at the end of 1920 and 111 a year later, as prices fell first; the wage cuts of 1922 took them back to 97, and as prices then fell faster than money rates they reached 115 at the end of 1934. On the 1924 base, money rates fell to 94.0 in 1933 and real rates rose to 110.7 in 1933 and 117.2 in 1938. The Ministry's later index, on four bases from September 1939, is drawn in "Real wage rates, 1935-1975"; wages before 1861 in "Wages in towns, 1790-1860".

title: Real wage rates, 1935-1975
unit_long: index of wage rates over prices
note: The Ministry of Labour's index of weekly full-time wage rates (all workers, all industries and services; later titled the index of basic wage rates of manual workers, from 1970 the Department of Employment's) at the end of June each year, divided by the year's Retail Prices Index (ONS long-run series), 1939 = 100. The index was based four times: 1 September 1939, 30 June 1947, 31 January 1956 and 31 July 1972; the bases are joined by the levels the Annual Abstract prints (June 1947 between 167 and 168 on the 1939 base, revised from 166-167; January 1956 by the factor 1.561; July 1972 249.5 on the 1956 base), and the weights change at each (marked). Rates, not earnings (war work raised earnings well above rates). Real rates fell to 94 in 1941 as prices rose faster, were back to 100 in 1947, fell again to 95 in 1952, then rose almost every year: 110 in 1960, 121 in 1970 and 152 in 1975 (money rates rose 82% from June 1972 to June 1975, yearly prices 57% from 1972 to 1975).

title: Average weekly earnings at 2025 prices, 1963-2025
label: 2000-2025 (KAB9)
note: Average weekly earnings, whole economy, total pay (ONS series KAB9), yearly, at 2025 prices (divided by the Retail Prices Index). Earnings, not rates: they include bonuses and overtime and change with the mix of jobs. The RPI rises faster than the official CPI and CPIH (the ONS no longer counts it a national statistic), so the fall since 2007 is larger here than on those measures. £313 a week in 2000 was £740 at 2025 prices; earnings peaked at £819 in 2007, fell to £711 in 2023 and were £728 in 2025. Dashed, 1963-1999: the ONS's long run back series of average weekly earnings, which the ONS gives "with a warning stating clearly that they are modelled estimates and do not come with the same methodological assurances on quality as estimates from January 2000 onwards" ("produced using the VAR model" of its methodology paper; not seasonally adjusted, each year the mean of its months). £10.92 a week in 1963 was £321 at 2025 prices; real earnings fell only in 1976-77 and 1995; they rose 50% from 1963 to 1975 (real wage rates, on the 1935-1975 graph, 35%: earnings also count overtime, bonuses and better-paid jobs) and 54% from 1975 to 1999 (£741 in 1999); the 1999 figure is £1 above the 2000 figure of the main line.

title: Merchant fleet registered in the UK, 1848-1970
label: All ships (from 1939 steam and motor)
note: Merchant ships registered in the United Kingdom (with the Channel Islands and the Isle of Man) at the end of each year, net tons, from the Statistical Abstract (Nos. 10, 13, 26, 32, 45, 46, 59, 70, 83): steam, motor (shown apart from 1924, with steam before) and sailing. Steam (net) tonnage overtook sail in 1883. The fleet grew from 3.4 million tons in 1848 (0.15 million of them steam) to 5.8 million in 1865, 7.4 million in 1884 and 12.4 million in 1914, lost 2.3 million in the First World War (to 1918), was 11.8 million in 1922, 12.5 million in 1930 and 10.7 million in 1938; sail peaked at 4.9 million in 1865 and fell to 0.4 million in 1938. From 1923 ships registered in the Irish Free State are left out; steamers' net tonnage rose slightly in 1914 when the Merchant Shipping Act 1907 came fully into force. From 1939 the line comes from the Annual Abstract (Ministry of Transport, later the Board of Trade): steam and motor vessels only, as it no longer counts sail each year (sailing vessels and other craft without engines: 414,000 net tons in 1935, 278,243 in 1966); its footnotes say that the figures for 1939-1962 include Commonwealth and foreign vessels on bareboat charter to or requisitioned by the United Kingdom. The fleet fell to 9.0 million net tons in 1942 and was 10.3 million in 1946, 12.0 million in 1961, 11.5 million in 1962 (its gross tonnage hardly changed: 21.90 and 21.94 million) and 14.7 million in 1970 (an estimate in No. 108). Vessels under 500 gross tons rose from 9,134 in 1935 to 21,200 in 1970 (No. 104: "including miscellaneous craft"). After 1970 the Annual Abstract gives only ships of 500 gross tons and over: see "UK-registered trading fleet".

title: UK-registered trading fleet, 1950-2025
label: All trading vessels
note: Trading vessels (carrying cargo or passengers) of 500 gross tons and over registered in the United Kingdom, the Channel Islands and the Isle of Man at the end of each year, million gross tons, from the Department for Transport's table FLE0301: all, tankers and (from 1969) container ships. To 1974 these are the Annual Abstract's "United Kingdom merchant vessels of 500 gross tons and over" (Nos. 109, 110, 112, read from the page images: DfT gives the same number, gross tons and tankers in every year but 1962-1963, which it has revised slightly). The fleet was 17.2 million gross tons (3,092 ships) in 1950, 20.5 million in 1961, and grew with its tankers to 31.5 million in 1975 (1,682 ships; tankers 17.1 million in 1975), then fell to 8.0 million in 1986 and 4.7 million in 1993 (344 ships); it was 30.5 million in 2017 and 18.8 million in 2025 (421 ships, 4.3 million of them container ships). The gross tons of the register graph to 1970 count every steam and motor ship of 500 gross tons and over, trading or not (21.2 million in 1961); these trading vessels are fewer.
